title: Structural Design Pattern Introduction
summary: Structural patterns are composition rules for wiring objects into larger systems — what each of the seven does, what it costs, and how to pick one in an interview.

refs.title: Understanding Structural Design Patterns in Java | by Pallavi Devraye

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: Creational patterns decide **what gets made**. Structural patterns decide **how finished pieces are wired together**. If your problem is incompatible interfaces, exploding subclasses, tangled dependencies, or too many objects — that is structural territory. Every one of these seven buys flexibility by adding **one level of indirection**, and every one charges you indirection as the price.
What it is, precisely

A structural pattern is a named way to compose classes and objects into a larger shape without rewriting the parts. The parts stay as they are — a legacy payment client, a rendering engine, a subsystem with 40 classes — and you add a wrapper, a layer, a tree node, or a shared cache in front of or around them so the client sees the shape it wants. The mechanism is almost always **object composition**: hold a reference to the wrapped object and forward, translate, fan out, or intercept calls. Inheritance appears only to keep the outward type identical, so the caller cannot tell wrapper from wrapped.

This is why structural patterns sit apart from the other two families. Creational patterns hide **construction logic** — who calls `new` and with what arguments. Behavioral patterns hide **interaction logic** — who calls whom, when, and how state propagates. Structural patterns hide **wiring logic** — what type the client talks to versus what type actually does the work. In an interview, that distinction is your triage tool. If the interviewer says “these two classes cannot talk to each other,” “this class hierarchy is exploding,” “this API is too complex to use,” or “we have ten million of these objects,” you are being pointed at Adapter, Bridge, Facade, or Flyweight before you write a line.
The mechanism: indirection with a purpose

blocks.title: Where each wrapper sits
blocks.caption: Every structural pattern inserts something between client and work. The difference is why.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    C1[Client] --> AD[Adapter]
    AD --> AE[Adaptee]
    C2[Client] --> FA[Facade]
    FA --> S1[SubsystemA]
    FA --> S2[SubsystemB]
    FA --> S3[SubsystemC]
    C3[Client] --> PR[Proxy]
    PR --> RE[RealSubject]
    C4[Client] --> DE[Decorator]
    DE --> CO[Component]
    AB[Abstraction] --> IM[Implementation]
    RO[Root] --> N1[Node]
    RO --> LF[Leaf]

blocks.text: Read the diagram left to right as **client intent versus hidden reality**. Adapter exists because the client demands interface X and the existing code only speaks Y, so the adapter translates in the middle — the trade-off is a translation layer you must now maintain. Facade exists because the client should not see 40 subsystem classes, so one simplified front cuts the dependency fan-out — the trade-off is that the facade becomes a magnet for unrelated convenience methods. Proxy and Decorator look identical in a class diagram — both hold a reference to the same interface they implement — but their **why** diverges: a proxy controls **access** to the object (lazy load, permission check, cache, remote hop) while a decorator adds **behavior** (extra rendering, extra cost calculation, extra stream processing). Confuse those two whys and you will pick the right shape for the wrong reason, which interviewers penalise harder than picking no pattern at all.
The seven patterns in one map

blocks.caption: The full structural set. Memorise the problem each one owns, not its UML.
rows: Adapter
Two ready-made interfaces do not fit
Wrap adaptee, expose target interface, translate calls
Bridge
Abstraction x implementation is exploding into N x M subclasses
Split into two hierarchies joined by composition
Composite
Client should treat one object and a group identically
Recursive tree where leaf and composite share one interface
Decorator
Need to add responsibilities per-object at runtime
Stackable wrappers, each adds one behavior then forwards
Facade
Subsystem is correct but unusable directly
Single simplified entry point that delegates inward
Flyweight
Too many fine-grained objects exhaust memory
Split intrinsic shared state from extrinsic per-use state, share the rest
Proxy
Direct access is wrong: too slow, unsafe, or remote
Stand-in with same interface that gates or defers to the real object

blocks.text: Group them by intent and you stop memorising seven isolated definitions. **Adapter and Facade simplify what exists**: Adapter fixes one mismatched interface, Facade flattens a whole subsystem. Both are usually thin and stateless, which is why they are safe to introduce late. **Bridge and Composite organise growth**: Bridge stops a Cartesian explosion of subclasses by turning one axis into composition, Composite turns ad-hoc tree-walking code into uniform recursion. Both require you to see the second axis or the tree early — retrofit either after the hierarchy has calcified and you will rewrite callers anyway. **Decorator, Proxy, and Flyweight manage cost at runtime**: per-object behavior, per-access control, per-instance memory. Those three are the only ones where the payoff depends on load, latency, or memory pressure, so never justify them with aesthetics. Justify them with numbers.
The trade-offs, honestly

blocks.caption: Each pattern charges the same currency: indirection.
rows: Decouples client from concrete structure
Extra types, extra forwarding, harder stack traces
When 3+ wrappers stack for one call, you over-applied Decorator or Proxy
Lets independently built code collaborate
Translation code rots when either side evolves
Adapter on a churning third-party API needs version pins and contract tests
Kills N x M subclass explosion
Two hierarchies to understand instead of one
Bridge with only one implementation is pure overhead — use plain inheritance
Uniform treatment of part and whole
Type safety weakens: every node exposes child operations
Composite where leaf-only operations throw at runtime is a design smell
Simpler client code
Facade hides power the advanced caller still needs
Facade without an escape hatch to the subsystem forces bypass hacks
Large memory or latency savings
Shared mutable state and cache-invalidation bugs
Flyweight or caching Proxy without a clear ownership story corrupts data

blocks.text: The meta-trade-off is this: structural patterns **move complexity, they do not remove it**. Adapter moves mismatch pain from every caller into one translator. Facade moves navigation pain from every caller into one entry point. Bridge moves subclass pain into a composition seam. Decorator moves feature-combination pain into wrapper ordering. The design is better only if the new location is cheaper to change than the old one. That is the sentence senior interviewers wait for. Juniors say “Decorator adds behavior flexibly.” Seniors say “Decorator adds per-object behavior without subclass explosion, at the cost of ordering-sensitive stacks and identity confusion — `decorated == original` is false and debugging gets harder.” Always attach the cost to the benefit in the same breath.
How it fails in production

Structural failures are quiet. Nothing throws on deploy. What degrades is debuggability, memory, or change velocity. The classic is the **decorator stack nobody can unwind**: logging, metrics, retry, auth, compression wrapped six deep around a stream or HTTP client. Each wrapper is correct in isolation. Together they allocate on every request, swallow the original stack frame, and make ordering load-bearing — swap retry and timeout and your timeout never fires. The symptom you see is p99 latency creep plus logs that name the wrapper, never the root cause. The second classic is the **leaky facade**: one `Utils` or `ServiceManager` front that started as five delegating methods and grew to eighty, importing half the codebase. The symptom is a merge-conflict hotspot and circular dependencies radiating from the one class that was supposed to reduce coupling. The third is the **shared-state flyweight or caching proxy**: intrinsic state that was assumed immutable turns out to be mutable, or a proxy cache with no invalidation policy. The symptom is cross-request contamination — user A sees user B’s glyph, price, or permission — intermittent, unreproducible locally, and always blamed on the database first.

items: Stack traces full of `Proxy`, `Wrapper`, `Delegate` frames and no business frame — proxy or decorator overuse.
Memory flat but GC thrashing on object creation — missing Flyweight where intrinsic state repeats millions of times.
`instanceof` and downcasts scattered after a Composite — the uniform interface was a lie; leaf and composite diverged.
Adapter with `if version == 2` branches inside translate methods — the adapted API moved and the adapter became a compatibility dump.
Facade importing UI, persistence, and networking packages at once — it stopped being a facade and became a god object.
Bridge where abstraction calls `if (impl instanceof X)` — the decoupling failed; the abstraction knows its implementation again.

blocks.title: The over-wrapping trap
blocks.text: If you cannot name what each wrapper **adds or gates** in one clause, delete it. A Decorator that only forwards is dead code. A Proxy that neither checks, caches, defers, nor remotes anything is a slower direct call. Interviewers will ask you to remove layers, not just add them.
Code that makes the difference concrete

Adapter and Decorator share the same skeleton — implement the expected interface, hold the wrapped object, forward — and differ only in intent. That is exactly why interviews test them together. Below is the minimal Java that exposes the distinction. The adapter translates a mismatched method; the decorator keeps the method and augments the result. Notice both pay forwarding cost, but for opposite reasons: the adapter pays it once to reconcile two teams that never agreed on a type, the decorator pays it per layer to avoid a subclass for every feature mix.

Why this wiring matters: swapping the two wrappers changes nothing structurally and everything semantically. `TimingRenderer` around `PlotterAdapter` times translation plus plotting, which is what you want for latency budgets. An adapter around a decorator would mean translating an already-augmented interface — usually a sign the layer order is wrong. The same ordering logic governs Bridge versus Adapter, the pair candidates confuse most. Adapter is **retroactive**: the two sides already exist and disagree, so you patch after the fact. Bridge is **proactive**: you foresee two axes of change — say `Shape` (circle, square) varying independently from `DrawingAPI` (vector, raster) — and you insert the seam before the N x M explosion happens. Adapter rescues; Bridge prevents. Say that distinction verbatim in the interview.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Name the seam, not the pattern
items.text: Start with: “The client wants X but the code provides Y, so I need a translation / simplification / interception point here.” Then map it: mismatch is Adapter, simplification is Facade, access control is Proxy, per-object addition is Decorator. Interviewers score the diagnosis above the label.

items.title: Draw the forwarding arrow
items.text: Sketch client → wrapper → wrapped on the board and state who holds whom. If you cannot draw the reference direction without hesitation, you do not understand the pattern yet. This one diagram separates memorised definitions from working knowledge.

items.title: Defend with the trade-off
items.text: Follow every proposal with its cost: “Facade cuts 40 imports to 1, but risks becoming a god object, so I will scope it per use-case and leave an escape hatch.” No trade-off stated means no senior signal.

items.title: Handle the follow-up pivot
items.text: Expect: “Now add caching / permissions / listing children / undo.” Caching or permission on top of direct access is Proxy. Children enumeration on a flat map forces Composite. Undo stacked on behavior forces Decorator versus Command — argue it. The follow-up tests whether your first choice survives growth.

items.title: Kill your darlings on request
items.text: Expect: “We only have two shapes and one renderer — still use Bridge?” The correct answer is no. Bridge with one implementation, Flyweight with a thousand objects, Facade over three methods — all overhead. Saying when not to use it earns more points than applying it.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail you

items: **“Adapter and Facade are the same.”** No. Adapter fixes *one* interface to match what the client already expects. Facade defines a *new, smaller* interface over many classes. Adapter conforms; Facade simplifies.

**“Decorator is just inheritance.”** Inheritance adds behavior to a *class* for all instances at compile time. Decorator adds behavior to an *object* at runtime, stackably. If the mix varies per request, inheritance needs 2^N subclasses — that is the exact pain Decorator exists to avoid.

**“Proxy and Decorator are interchangeable.”** Same UML, opposite purpose. Proxy gates access to the *same* behavior (lazy, protect, cache, remote). Decorator extends behavior. Ask: does it do more, or does it guard the way in?

**“Bridge is just Adapter done early.”** Adapter reconciles existing incompatibility. Bridge anticipates two independent axes of change and separates them up front. One is a patch, the other is a planned seam.

**“Composite is just a list of children.”** A list does not give uniform treatment. Composite’s whole point is that client code calls `draw()` or `cost()` without caring leaf versus group. If callers still branch on type, you built a tree, not a Composite.

**“Flyweight is just caching.”** Caching stores computed results. Flyweight shares *intrinsic* immutable state across instances and pushes *extrinsic* state to the caller. The memory win comes from the split, not from the map.

blocks.title: What the interviewer is listening for
blocks.text: Three sentences: which mismatch or explosion you saw, which seam you inserted, and what that seam costs. Example: “`CirclePNG`, `CircleSVG`, `SquarePNG` is an N x M explosion, so I split `Shape` from `Renderer` with a Bridge — two hierarchies instead of six classes, at the price of one more hop per draw.” That is a pass.
When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Use structural patterns as targeted fixes, not default architecture.
rows: Integrating legacy or third-party code you cannot change
Adapter to translate at the boundary
Editing the third-party class or forking it per caller
Two dimensions vary independently (shape x renderer, notification x sender)
Bridge to compose instead of multiplying subclasses
Bridge when one axis has a single implementation
Part-whole hierarchies (files, UI, org charts, graphics)
Composite for uniform recursive operations
Composite when leaf and group operations never overlap
Optional behaviors mixed per object at runtime
Decorator for stackable additions
Decorator when the stack order is load-bearing and undocumented
Subsystem with dozens of entry points
Facade scoped per use-case
Single global Facade that every team extends
Millions of small objects with repeated state
Flyweight splitting intrinsic from extrinsic state
Flyweight when objects are few or shared state is mutable
Expensive, remote, or sensitive access
Proxy for lazy, protection, cache, or remote stand-in
Proxy that only forwards with no check or deferral

blocks.text: The easy-difficulty label on this topic is misleading. Reciting seven definitions is easy; choosing the one seam that survives the follow-up is not. Default stance: start with the simplest direct call, introduce Adapter the moment two teams disagree on a type, Facade the moment a caller imports more than it understands, Bridge the moment you catch yourself naming classes `X_Y`, Composite the moment callers branch on leaf versus group, Decorator the moment feature mixes multiply, Proxy the moment access needs a gate, Flyweight the moment a profiler shows memory dominated by duplicated immutable state. Each introduction must be reversible — if the pressure never materialises, remove the layer. Simplicity that can grow beats structure that must be undone.

blocks.title: Say this in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Structural patterns compose existing objects into larger usable shapes — Adapter translates, Bridge decouples axes, Composite unifies part and whole, Decorator stacks behavior, Facade simplifies, Flyweight shares, Proxy gates — each trading one hop of indirection for flexibility you should only pay for when you need it.
